newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Growing Hungary debt issue not seen harming economy.
newsitem.headline: Growing Hungary debt issue not seen harming economy.

text.p: Hungary's gross domestic debt issue will double next year but this is not expected to depress the economy, the Government Debt Management Agency (AKK) said on Tuesday.

Gross domestic government security issues will amount to 1,800 to 1,900 billion forints next year, up from 922 billion forint planned for 1996, AKK Deputy Director Laszlo Borbely told a news conference.

The debt issues will be boosted partly by changes in accounting for the foreign state debt, 2,000 billion forints worth of which will be transferred from the National Bank of Hungary (NBH) to the state budget from January 1.

AKK Deputy Director Maria Dunavolgyi said the change aims at making the state budget more transparent in order to meet the requirements of the European Union, which Hungary would like to join around 2000, as well as at reducing inflation risks.
"Central bank financing involves infinite inflation risks," she said.

Government officials earlier said the change is purely technical. The NBH will formally remain the debtor of all its creditors until the loans mature, and no economic policy adjustment will be demanded by the debt transfer.

Borbely said the economy will not be harmed by the change as net debt issue will hardly grow next year from 1997 as large amounts of state debt will mature and investors usually reinvest funds from matured government securities.
"Three-quarters of (maturing debt) is discount Treasury bills which is automatically reinvested, while most of the interest is also reinvested," he said.

The AKK's net debt issue target for next year is 360 to 380 billion forints, up from 310 to 320 billion forints planned for 1996, but this increase is not likely to push up interest rates and inflation, the AKK said.
"This increase is not substantial," AKK Director Zsuzsanna Acs said. "If we look at the real value, this is smaller than inflation."

However, the plans about next year's issue could be fulfilled only if Hungary's inflation and interest rates are not increased above the government target by other factors than the state debt, Borbely added.
Hungary plans to reduce inflation to 18 percent next year from the latest official forecast of 22 to 24 percent for 1996.
